analysis.one_liner: Eliminates federal income tax on profits from selling pre-2008 distressed mortgages and mortgage securities.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and never received a vote, dying when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the tax code so that anyone who bought a residential or commercial mortgage, or a security backed by such a mortgage, issued on or before March 14, 2008, could sell it after holding it for more than a year and pay no federal tax on the profit [S2][S3]. It applied only to assets bought after enactment and before January 1, 2009, and sales to relatives or related companies would not count [S2][S3]. It was introduced October 3, 2008, at the height of the financial crisis, and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, where it received no further action [S1][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Investors, banks, hedge funds, and other buyers of distressed pre-2008 mortgages and mortgage-backed securities, who could sell those assets after a year and keep their gains completely free of federal income tax. The stated rationale was to encourage private capital to absorb troubled assets during the 2008 crisis, but the direct beneficiaries were the holders who sold.

how_it_helps.text: Would exclude from gross income any gain from selling or exchanging a qualified mortgage or mortgage-related security held for more than one year [S2][S3].

Covers residential and commercial mortgages plus any security or instrument based on them, as long as the mortgage was originated on or before March 14, 2008 and the taxpayer bought the asset after enactment and before January 1, 2009 [S2][S3].
Would encourage private investors to purchase troubled mortgage assets at the height of the 2008 financial crisis by making resale profits tax-free.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through lost Treasury revenue. Every dollar of gain that sellers exclude from income is a dollar not taxed, and the exclusion has no dollar cap, so large trades by large institutions produce large revenue losses. Homeowners facing foreclosure get no direct relief.

drawbacks.text: The tax exclusion is unlimited in size and applies to commercial as well as residential mortgages, so the largest gains — and the largest revenue losses — would go to the biggest financial institutions and investors [S3].
The bill gives nothing directly to distressed homeowners or to anyone facing foreclosure; the benefit flows entirely to buyers and sellers of the assets built on those mortgages [S3].

Because it covers anything 'based on or related to' a pre-2008 mortgage, including complex securities, the benefit would reach holders of precisely the mortgage-backed instruments at the center of the 2008 crisis, rewarding resale of bad assets with a tax windfall [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The stated idea — coaxing private capital into buying troubled mortgage assets during the 2008 panic — had a real logic. But the design is one-sided: a completely uncapped income-tax exclusion on resale gains, covering commercial as well as residential mortgages, with no requirement that any benefit reach borrowers or neighborhoods. Whatever stabilizing effect cheaper tax treatment of these trades might have had would come at the price of a pure windfall to whoever was positioned to buy low and sell high, paid for by ordinary taxpayers. No action was ever taken on the bill, so those tradeoffs were never tested in committee or on the floor.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it expired when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Bill Sali introduced the bill on October 3, 2008, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means [S1][S5].
No further action was ever taken; the bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Taxpayers, since no revenue was lost. Financial institutions and investors who might have sold distressed mortgage securities tax-free gained nothing, and the asset-purchase incentive the bill offered never materialized.

for.name: Rep. Bill Sali
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Ways and Means Committee.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral with jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; it never received a markup or a vote.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill had zero cosponsors, so there was no recorded partisan division — only a single Republican sponsor and no committee action [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Banks, hedge funds, and investors in mortgage-backed securities
industries.note: The bill would let them sell pre-2008 mortgage assets and mortgage-related securities after a year without paying federal income tax on the gain — an uncapped windfall financed by taxpayers. Its stated purpose was to pull private capital into troubled assets during the 2008 crisis, which could have modestly supported credit and housing markets, but no benefit flows to borrowers or homeowners directly.
Every excluded gain is revenue the Treasury would otherwise collect, with no dollar cap in the bill; the cost of the incentive falls on ordinary taxpayers.
